## Solution

**Preliminary observation on well-posedness.** The integrand $f(z)=\dfrac{1}{\sin z}$ has simple poles exactly at the zeros of $\sin z$, namely $z=n\pi$ for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. The set $\{\pi n:n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}\}=\{\ldots,-2\pi,-\pi,\pi,2\pi,\ldots\}$ is **unbounded**. A simple closed contour $\gamma$ is compact, hence its interior is bounded, so it **cannot** enclose the entire unbounded set $\{\pi n:n\neq 0\}$. Taken literally the hypothesis is therefore impossible.

The only well-posed reading consistent with "encloses the origin" and the use of Cauchy's residue theorem is that $\gamma$ encloses the origin (the pole at $z=0$) together with **finitely many** of the nonzero poles $\pi n$. We compute the integral under this interpretation; the value is determined by which poles lie inside $\gamma$.

---

**Residues of $\csc z$.** Near a zero $z_0=n\pi$ of $\sin z$ we have
$$\sin z = \sin(n\pi + (z-n\pi)) = (-1)^{n}\sin(z-n\pi) = (-1)^{n}\bigl((z-n\pi) - \tfrac{(z-n\pi)^{3}}{3!}+\cdots\bigr).$$
Thus $\sin z = (-1)^{n}(z-n\pi)\bigl(1+O((z-n\pi)^{2})\bigr)$, so $z=n\pi$ is a simple zero and
$$\operatorname{Res}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sin z},\,n\pi\right)=\lim_{z\to n\pi}\frac{z-n\pi}{\sin z}=\frac{1}{(-1)^{n}\cos(n\pi)}\cdot\frac{1}{1}=\frac{1}{(-1)^{n}}=(-1)^{n}.$$
(Equivalently, $\operatorname{Res}(\csc z,n\pi)=1/\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^{n}$.)

In particular the residue at the origin is
$$\operatorname{Res}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sin z},\,0\right)=(-1)^{0}=1.$$

---

**Applying Cauchy's residue theorem.** Let $S\subset\mathbb{Z}$ be the finite set of indices $n$ for which $n\pi$ lies in the interior of $\gamma$; by hypothesis $0\in S$. Since $\gamma$ is a simple closed positively oriented contour and $1/\sin z$ is holomorphic on and inside $\gamma$ except at the poles $\{n\pi:n\in S\}$, Cauchy's residue theorem gives
$$\oint_{\gamma}\frac{1}{\sin z}\,dz=2\pi i\sum_{n\in S}\operatorname{Res}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sin z},\,n\pi\right)=2\pi i\sum_{n\in S}(-1)^{n}.$$

---

**The standard case: $\gamma$ encloses only the origin.** In the most common formulation of this problem the contour encloses the single pole at $z=0$ and no other pole, i.e. $S=\{0\}$. Then
$$\oint_{\gamma}\frac{1}{\sin z}\,dz=2\pi i\cdot(-1)^{0}=2\pi i\cdot 1=\boxed{2\pi i}.$$

---

**Remark on the symmetric case.** If instead $\gamma$ encloses the symmetric block of poles $\{-N\pi,\ldots,-\pi,0,\pi,\ldots,N\pi\}$, then $S=\{-N,\ldots,N\}$ and
$$\sum_{n=-N}^{N}(-1)^{n}=1+2\sum_{n=1}^{N}(-1)^{n}=\begin{cases}1,&N\text{ even},\\ -1,&N\text{ odd},\end{cases}$$
so the integral would be $2\pi i$ or $-2\pi i$ depending on $N$—confirming that a definite value requires specifying which poles are enclosed. Under the canonical interpretation (only the origin enclosed), the value is $2\pi i$.
